column1: # Mock community definitions for amphid
# What went into each mock well, declared BEFORE sequencing. This is the
# only file in the pipeline that states an expected answer, and it is what
# makes amplification efficiency measurable rather than assumed.
# Validate it against the panel and samplesheet while designing the plate:
#   python3 bin/preflight.py --reference panel.tsv --samplesheet samples.csv \
#       --runs runs.tsv --mocks mocks.tsv --assay assets/assay/...json \
#       --outdir check
# COLUMNS
#   sample_id     must appear in the samplesheet with sample_type = mock
#   seq_id        a reference in the panel
#   amount        how much of it went in. Units are declared per row by
#                 amount_units; every row of one sample must agree
#   amount_units  copies | fraction | ng
#                 copies   absolute molecules added (best - ties the mock
#                          to the same scale as the quant standards)
#                 fraction proportion of the target mixture, summing to 1
#                          across the sample's target rows
#                 ng       mass; converted to copies only if the panel
#                          carries a length, otherwise treated as relative
#   mix           a label shared by every well of the same intended
#                 mixture, e.g. "TriPair_90_10". Replicates of one mix
#                 share the label; this is what the calibrator groups on
#   replicate     1, 2, 3 ... distinguishes wells within a mix
#   pcr_batch     which PCR occasion this well was amplified in. Wells from
#                 one plate share a batch. Without this the calibrator
#                 cannot separate systematic bias from one bad plate, and
#                 the confidence interval on corr_factor is meaningless
#   note          free text
# DESIGN NOTES - these determine whether the data can answer the question
#   Use a RATIO SERIES, not a single 50/50 mix. Amplification bias is not
#   guaranteed to be a per-species constant: templates compete for primers
#   and polymerase, so the observed ratio can compress toward the middle as
#   one species dominates. A single mix gives one point, no slope, and a
#   correction that is right only at the ratio you happened to mock - and
#   real samples are mostly one dominant species plus a minority, which is
#   exactly where a mid-ratio constant fails.
#   The calibrator tests this directly: log(observed ratio) against
#   log(input ratio). Slope 1 means a per-species constant is valid and the
#   intercept is it. Slope below 1 means compression, and a constant will
#   overstate every minority species. You need at least three ratios per
#   pair to see a slope, and five is better.
#   INCLUDE THE QUANT STANDARDS in every mock. corr_factor is defined
#   relative to them. A mock without them yields efficiencies that float
#   against each other but are not anchored to the scale field samples are
#   measured on, and they cannot be transferred.
#   MATCH THE PCR to the real assay - same cycle number, polymerase, input
#   mass, master mix lot. Competition bias grows as reagents deplete, so a
#   mock at 30 cycles does not predict bias at 40.
#   REPLICATE ACROSS PCR OCCASIONS, not just across wells. Three wells on
#   one plate measure pipetting. Three separate PCRs measure the thing you
#   are trying to correct for.
#   The extreme ratios pay for themselves twice: a 99/1 mix also measures
#   the minority limit of quantification - the smallest real minority that
#   can be told from index hopping and chimera background.
#   WHAT THIS DOES NOT MEASURE. Plasmid or gDNA mocks mixed before PCR
#   measure amplification bias alone. Extraction and lysis bias are
#   untouched, so a corr_factor derived here corrects one step of three
#   when applied to eggs in stool. Record that with the number.
